item.title: Stocks sway as Wall Street heads for a winning week after several turbulent days
item.description: Stocks are mixed in morning trading Friday as Wall Street heads for its first winning week since early October, despite days of big swings led by AI-focused companies.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: U.S. stocks closed lower Friday as a pullback in big AI-focused companies weighed on the market, capping a turbulent week on Wall Street. The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent, but managed to post a 2.5 per cent gain for the week. This marks the benchmark index’s first winning week since October and its biggest weekly gain since August. The Dow Jones Industrial Average recovered from an early slide and eked out a 0.1 per cent gain. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.9 per cent, but also notched its first weekly gain in five weeks. The major indexes have been shaky this week as some of the biggest AI companies pushed and pulled the market. Many of those companies have big stock values with a heavier impact on the market’s gains or losses. The market remained unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The company has been the face of the AI industry, which has been responsible for much of the gains, and big swings, on Wall Street. Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns. Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO. The ensuing fallout cost Nvidia’s market cap more than US$600 billion this week. The AI industry’s influence over Wall Street was evident again Friday, as the slump in technology stocks with a big focus on AI weighed on the market, even though more than 60 per cent of the stocks within the S&P 500 rose. Nvidia was again among the heaviest weights and it fell 2 per cent. Broadcom fell 4.8 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 8.8 per cent. Both companies saw their shares surge earlier this week as the management shake-up at Nvidia unfolded. Nvidia in particular has been slipping for weeks amid wider concerns about a potential slowdown for the industry. The big worry has been whether AI will produce enough profit to justify the costly investments and big stock values. “Nvidia’s pullback serves as a reminder of the concentration risk embedded in a market where a small number of mega-cap technology stocks have driven an outsized share of returns,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note. Outside of AI, Microsoft rose 0.2 per cent, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications. Among the gainers were healthcare and financial stocks. Eli Lilly and Co. rose 1.3 per cent. Payment processors Visa and Mastercard also closed 1.3 per cent higher. All told, the S&P 500 fell 30.73 points to 7,561.67. The index is up 10.5 per cent so far this year. The Dow gained 50.46 points to 52,347.55, and the Nasdaq gave up 229.82 points to close at 25,136.27. Oil prices swung a day after President Donald Trump said that the U.S. didn’t “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It settled at US$95.84 a barrel. It was trading near US$72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began. Stocks in Europe were mixed. Treasury yields were mixed in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 5.15 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. The yield on the two-year Treasury rose to 4.87 per cent from 4.86 per cent late Thursday. It closely tracks expectations for action from the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting in an effort to cool stubbornly hot inflation. A report on Friday showed that wholesale inflation cooled a bit last month, but remains very high. The report measures inflation experienced by businesses, before it can reach consumers. Inflation at the consumer level remains stubbornly high at well above 3 per cent. That’s also much higher than the Fed’s preferred target of 2 per cent. Rising energy prices because of the U.S. war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising. The latest wholesale inflation report also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs. “That suggests inflation is working its way into the broader economy rather than remaining concentrated in the original areas of price pressure,” said Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, in a research note. “If that continues, it becomes much harder for the Fed to simply look through inflation as temporary.” The central bank held rates steady at its last meeting, following a previous rate hike. The latest hot updates on inflation have prompted economists to overwhelmingly expect a rate hike at the upcoming December meeting, with another hike likely to follow in January. Rate hikes by the Fed can cool inflation, but that makes borrowing more expensive and can slow economic growth. ___ Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Chan Ho-Him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: Investor Outlook: AI helps accelerate quantum computing development
item.description: Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook discusses Canada’s quantum computing ambitions, third-quarter results and the path to commercial growth.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Canada’s quantum computing ambitions are drawing attention to the country’s ability to turn research into a globally competitive industry. The federal budget has put the sector’s future in sharper focus. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO at Xanadu, about Canada’s position in quantum computing, the company’s third-quarter results and its development plans. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: ROGER: Last week’s federal budget singled out Xanadu by name as a critical investment alongside Cohere for Canada to maintain its sovereignty. Let’s find out what it will take for companies like Xanadu to scale and compete on the global stage. Joining me now is Christian Weedbrook, the founder and CEO of Xanadu. Christian, good to see you. How are you? CHRISTIAN: I’m good, thank you. How are you? ROGER: Good. Let’s talk big picture. Being mentioned in a budget, a lot of pressure on you. Where do you see quantum fitting in? People are starting to grasp AI. I think quantum, though, is still, is still the next level. Where do you see it fitting in now and coming down the road? CHRISTIAN: Yeah, it was great to see Xanadu mentioned in the budget, as you mentioned. You know, I think the big thing that more and more people are realizing is the fact that, you know, quantum is going to be the next big thing after artificial intelligence. Folks are now very much familiar with AI and what it can do, and we see, you know, quantum computing as the next big thing after AI, and specifically, like something, if you look at the early days of the internet or early days of digital computing, that’s really where quantum computing sits. Xanadu is one of the leaders in the world, proudly Canadian, and we truly are on the world stage. ROGER: And where does it fit in with AI? Is it competition, or is it going to work together with it? CHRISTIAN: Really, we see it as working together, for sure. You know, along with it being the next big thing after AI, AI is not going anywhere. And to give you a great example, we use a lot of AI currently in building towards building a large-scale quantum computer. Some of the AI LLMs that we’ve used have really sped up our team’s progress by a year or more, which is quite phenomenal. So they go very well together, and we think that’s an, you know, really essential component to getting to a large-scale quantum computer that can really attract large amount of customers and, at that point, change the world. ROGER: And what would it mean for sovereignty here in Canada? CHRISTIAN: Yeah, I think that’s one of the reasons why we were mentioned in the budget. It’s a sovereign play. It’s really important. Specifically, we’re in the DARPA QBI program. Canada has its own version of the QBI program called the Canadian Quantum Champions Program, and that’s, I believe, what was mentioned in the budget. So the Canadian government has long invested in quantum computing through universities, probably for over two decades now, and Xanadu and other great companies in Canada are now leveraging that, you know, that seed that was planted in terms of the jobs. We had nearly 400 folks. Half of them, I believe, now, or over half, are actually from Canada. So we’ve done a great job in attracting the future workforce and talent by coming to Canada and staying here. ROGER: Is Canada, is Canada a centre for quantum? And are they keeping people? You say some people have come, but are we losing some as well? CHRISTIAN: No, I mean, on the overall, we’re definitely attracting the talent and keeping them here. They love Canada. They love the fact that, you know, that we have some world-class talent. Three of the Canadian companies, including Xanadu, are actually part of 11 companies in the DARPA QBI program. So we’re hitting a well above our body weight, and also funding. We have a lot of great investors that are investing, Canadian investors, and so I think that’s attracting some great talent. But overall, I think it’s, you know, Xanadu has had four Nature publications, two in the last year, and really the best talent want to see what the best talent is working on and come join them. And Xanadu is a great example of that. ROGER: And talking about where you’re at, I mean, your earnings report just came out, some big misses. What’s driving all that right now? I know you’re early. CHRISTIAN: Yeah, yeah, exactly. The main thing that we focus on is hardware development and hardware milestones and achieving them. And so, the biggest challenge for us and anyone else building quantum computers is errors. And we’re a photonic-based approach, and the errors really come from a loss and the loss of the photonic systems, essentially. So we focus on taking the opportunity for our earnings calls to reiterate that it’s all about technical milestones. Revenue is obviously key, but quantum computing is really the end result, is achieving a large-scale quantum computer by 2029, 2030. Other companies are doing great work, and they’re focusing, it seems like, some cases exclusively on revenue. We believe that, for us, the best approach is to focus on hardware milestones because in 2029, 2030, when we’re aiming to have our large-scale quantum computer, that’s when all bets are off, and that’s when true revenue actually occurs. And we think investors are investing in us because of our hardware milestones, our technical capabilities and our unique photonic-based approach. ROGER: And how are you doing with those milestones? What are you hitting right now? CHRISTIAN: Yeah, our milestones are on track. We announced three key optical loss demonstrations, and particularly we have what we believe is the world’s best low-loss optical switch. Optical switches are needed for our quantum computer, but they have far bigger, you know, currently far bigger applications in, in quant— in, in AI and data centres as well. So we’re really excited about that, and that’s a great example of where the team is hitting their hardware milestones when it comes to loss reduction. ROGER: Is that a possible revenue stream, then? Data centres before you, we get into the full quantum computers. CHRISTIAN: It is a possibility. As we mentioned on our earnings call, our relationship to revenue is as long as it doesn’t deviate from building a large-scale quantum computer, which is what our main focus is, then we’re definitely open to commercializing things. The reality is, Xanadu has, you know, arguably the best team in the world for extreme low-loss optical components. Things like AI, data centres, they’re becoming more and more relevant. So we do keep an eye on that, and it’s something that we’re definitely considering. ROGER: And what are some of the other milestones that you’ve been hitting, and what do they mean? CHRISTIAN: Yeah, some great partnerships. We announced partnerships with ASML. We believe we’re the only quantum company so far that’s actually working with ASML. We announced great partnerships with Bluefors as well, and all of these partnerships are helping us to achieve the ultimate vision of a large-scale quantum computer. Also, from the commercial side and partnerships and revenue side, some great partnerships with Mitsubishi as well. So the team is firing on all cylinders. I’m really excited of the future. ROGER: OK, Christian, thank you very much for joining us today. Appreciate it. CHRISTIAN: Thank you for having me. ROGER: Christian Weedbrook is the founder and CEO of Xanadu. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 13, 2026 interview with Christian Weedbrook are published with the assistance of AI. Original research, interview questions and added context was created by BNN Bloomberg journalists. An editor also reviewed this material before it was published to ensure its accuracy and adherence with BNN Bloomberg editorial policies and standards.
